stem: Where does Claude Desktop on macOS read its MCP server configuration from?

options.text: `~/Library/Application Support/Claude/claude_desktop_settings/mcp_servers.json`
options.why: No such file or folder exists; the config file sits directly in the `Claude` folder.

options.text: `~/Library/Application Support/Claude/claude_desktop_config.json`
options.why: Correct: Settings > Developer > Edit Config opens (or creates) this file.

options.text: `.vscode/mcp.json` in the open project
options.why: That is VS Code's workspace MCP configuration.

options.text: `~/Library/Logs/Claude/mcp.json`
options.why: That folder holds Claude Desktop's MCP log files, not its configuration.

explanation: Claude Desktop reads `claude_desktop_config.json`: `~/Library/Application Support/Claude/` on macOS and `%APPDATA%\Claude\` on Windows. Each host has its own file and format, which is a common source of copy-paste errors between Claude Desktop, Claude Code and VS Code.

stem: Which `claude_desktop_config.json` content correctly registers the filesystem server for two folders?

options.text: `{"servers": {"filesystem": {"command": "npx", "args": ["-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem", "/Users/me/Desktop"]}}}`
options.why: `servers` is VS Code's top-level key; Claude Desktop looks under `mcpServers`.

options.text: `{"mcpServers": {"filesystem": {"command": "npx -y @modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem /Users/me/Desktop /Users/me/Downloads"}}}`
options.why: The whole command line is crammed into `command`; the executable goes in `command` and each argument in the `args` array.

options.text: `{"mcpServers": {"filesystem": {"command": "npx", "args": ["-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem", "/Users/me/Desktop", "/Users/me/Downloads"]}}}`
options.why: Correct: `command` is the executable, `args` the argument list, under `mcpServers`.

options.text: `{"mcpServers": [{"name": "filesystem", "cmd": "npx", "argv": ["-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem"]}]}`
options.why: `mcpServers` is an object keyed by server name, and the fields are `command` and `args`.

explanation: A Claude Desktop entry lives under `mcpServers`, keyed by a friendly name. `command` is the program to launch, `args` its arguments (here the package and the directories the server may access), and an optional `env` object supplies environment variables. The host launches the process and talks to it over stdio.

stem: After you edit `claude_desktop_config.json`, closing the Claude Desktop window is enough for the new MCP servers to load.

options.text: True
options.why: Closing the window leaves the app running, so the old configuration stays loaded.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: you must fully quit Claude Desktop and start it again for configuration (or server code) changes to take effect.

explanation: Claude Desktop starts configured stdio servers when the application launches. The official guide says to completely quit and restart it after saving the config, and the debugging guide repeats that closing the window is not enough.

stem: What is the MCP Inspector?

options.text: A hosted registry that rates MCP servers for security before you install them
options.why: The MCP Registry stores server metadata; the Inspector is a local developer tool.

options.text: The reference tool for testing servers: call tools, read resources, watch traffic
options.why: Correct: it ships as a web UI, a CLI and a TUI in one package.

options.text: A proxy that sits in production between Claude and remote servers to block prompt injection
options.why: It is a development and debugging tool, not a production security gateway.

options.text: A VS Code extension that generates MCP server code from an OpenAPI specification
options.why: It does not generate servers; it connects to them like a client.

explanation: `@modelcontextprotocol/inspector` is the reference developer tool. It connects to stdio or Streamable HTTP servers, lets you invoke tools, prompts and resources by hand, and shows the JSON-RPC and HTTP traffic. The debugging guide calls it the first stop when a server misbehaves, before involving a real host and model.

stem:
Complete the Claude Code command that adds Notion's remote MCP server over Streamable HTTP:

```bash
claude mcp add --transport ____ notion https://mcp.notion.com/mcp
```

Type the missing transport value.
explanation: `claude mcp add --transport http <name> <url>` registers a remote Streamable HTTP server, which Claude Code recommends for remote servers. `--transport sse` exists for legacy SSE endpoints, and local servers use `--transport stdio` with the command after `--`. In JSON configuration the `type` field also accepts `streamable-http` as an alias for `http`.

stem: On macOS, a stdio server named `weather` misbehaves in Claude Desktop. Where do you find what the server wrote to stderr?

options.text: In `~/Library/Logs/Claude/mcp-server-weather.log`
options.why: Correct: per-server files capture each server's stderr, while `mcp.log` covers connections in general.

options.text: In the Claude chat window, where stderr appears as a system message
options.why: Stderr is not shown in the conversation; it goes to log files.

options.text: Nowhere, because a host throws away anything a stdio server writes to stderr
options.why: Hosts capture stderr; it is the right place for stdio server logs.

options.text: In `claude_desktop_config.json`, under a `logs` key that Claude adds to the entry
options.why: The config file is never used for logs.

explanation: Claude Desktop writes MCP logs to `~/Library/Logs/Claude` (macOS) or `%APPDATA%\Claude\logs` (Windows). `mcp.log` holds general connection logging and failures; `mcp-server-SERVERNAME.log` holds that server's stderr. Interviewers ask this to see whether you debug from evidence before changing code.

stem: Which of these products can act as an MCP host that connects to MCP servers? (Choose three.)

options.text: VS Code with GitHub Copilot
options.why: Listed among MCP clients, including support for extensions such as MCP Apps.

options.text: Cursor
options.why: An AI code editor that acts as an MCP client.

options.text: ChatGPT
options.why: Listed in the official extension client matrix as an MCP client.

options.text: PostgreSQL
options.why: A database. An MCP server can wrap it, but it does not host MCP clients.

options.text: Redis
options.why: A data store, not an AI application that connects to MCP servers.

options.text: nginx
options.why: A web server or reverse proxy; it may front an MCP server but is not a host.

explanation: MCP is vendor-neutral. Besides Claude's apps, hosts include VS Code GitHub Copilot, Cursor, ChatGPT, Goose, Postman, Microsoft 365 Copilot and many agent frameworks. Databases and proxies can sit behind or in front of servers, but a host is the AI application that creates MCP clients.

stem: What is the top-level key in `claude_desktop_config.json` under which local MCP servers are listed? Type the key.
explanation: Claude Desktop (and Claude Code's `.mcp.json`) use `mcpServers`, an object keyed by server name. VS Code's own `mcp.json` format uses `servers` instead, so pasting a config between hosts without renaming the key is a classic mistake.

stem: Put the steps for connecting Claude to a remote MCP server as a custom connector in order.

options.text: Choose Add, then Add custom connector
Complete the server's authentication prompts, typically OAuth
Open Settings and go to Connectors
Open the connector's settings to enable or disable specific tools
Enter the server's full `https://` URL and click Add

explanation: Remote servers are added through Custom Connectors in Claude or Claude Desktop rather than as local processes. After the URL comes the server's authentication (commonly OAuth), and the connector settings then let you control which tools Claude may use.

stem: Match each need with the Claude Code MCP configuration option that fits it.

options.text: Local scope
options.why: Default; stored in `~/.claude.json` under the current project; private to you.

options.text: Project scope
options.why: Stored in `.mcp.json` at the project root and checked into version control.

options.text: User scope
options.why: Stored in `~/.claude.json`; loads in all your projects; private to you.

options.text: Managed configuration
options.why: Deployed or provided by administrators for every user.

prompts.text: An experimental server with your personal API key, used only in this repository
A server every teammate should get automatically when they clone the repository
A personal utility server you want in every project on your machine
A server your IT team must roll out to every developer in the company

explanation: Scope controls where a server loads and whether it is shared. Local is the default and keeps credentials out of version control; project scope writes `.mcp.json` for the team (with an approval prompt before first use); user scope follows you across projects; managed configuration lets administrators provide servers centrally.

stem:
What does the `--` do in this command?

```bash
claude mcp add --env API_KEY=abc --transport stdio myserver -- python server.py --port 8080
```

options.text: It marks the start of the server's environment variables
options.why: Environment variables are given with `--env` before the name.

options.text: It tells Claude Code to run the server in the background
options.why: `--` has nothing to do with backgrounding.

options.text: It ends Claude Code's options; the rest launches the server
options.why: Correct: everything after `--` (including `--port 8080`) is passed to the server untouched.

options.text: It switches the transport from stdio to Streamable HTTP
options.why: The transport is set with `--transport`.

explanation: For stdio servers, `claude mcp add [options] <name> -- <command> [args...]`. Without the separator Claude Code would try to parse the server's own flags, such as `--port`, as its options. The MCP Inspector's web and TUI clients use a similar `--` convention for server arguments.

stem: A Python server starts fine when you run `python server.py` from its folder, but Claude Desktop reports it as failed. The config has `"command": "python", "args": ["./server.py"]`. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: Claude Desktop only supports servers written in Node.js
options.why: Any executable that speaks MCP over stdio works, including Python.

options.text: The relative path, since the host's working directory may be `/`
options.why: Correct: use absolute paths in the config and in any `.env` files.

options.text: The server must be started separately before Claude Desktop launches
options.why: The host launches stdio servers itself.

options.text: `args` must hold a single string, not an array
options.why: `args` is an array of arguments.

explanation: When a client launches a stdio server, the working directory may be undefined (for example `/` on macOS), because the client can be started from anywhere. The official troubleshooting steps include checking that paths are absolute, reading the logs, and running the exact command manually.

stem: Your server reads `GITHUB_TOKEN` from the environment. It works from a terminal where you exported the variable, but under Claude Desktop it fails with "token not set". What fixes it?

options.text: Export the variable again in your shell profile and restart the terminal
options.why: The host does not pass your shell's environment through, so profile changes do not help.

options.text: Add the token to the `args` array so it travels on the command line
options.why: That exposes the secret in process listings, and the server reads it from the environment anyway.

options.text: Write the token to stdout at startup so the host can capture it
options.why: Writing non-protocol data to stdout corrupts the stdio stream.

options.text: Set it in the entry's `env` object in the config file
options.why: Correct: stdio servers inherit only a limited set of environment variables.

explanation: MCP servers launched over stdio inherit only a platform-dependent subset of environment variables. Provide what the server needs through the `env` key of its config entry. The authorization spec likewise says stdio servers should take credentials from the environment rather than OAuth.

stem: In Claude Desktop, a file named `mcp-server-NAME.log` contains only the errors that the server reported.

options.text: True
options.why: It holds the server's whole stderr, not just errors.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: it contains everything the server wrote to stderr, and stdio servers often use stderr for all of their logging.

explanation: The per-server log captures stderr. Because stdout is reserved for protocol messages on stdio, servers send all diagnostics (info, debug and errors) to stderr, so the file is not limited to errors. `mcp.log` holds general connection logging.

stem: You paste a working Claude Desktop config into VS Code's `.vscode/mcp.json`, keeping `{"mcpServers": {...}}`. VS Code does not pick up the servers. Why?

options.text: VS Code only supports remote servers, not stdio ones
options.why: VS Code supports `"type": "stdio"` servers with `command` and `args`.

options.text: VS Code's format uses `servers`, not `mcpServers`
options.why: Correct: VS Code's configuration format uses `servers` (plus optional `inputs`).

options.text: The file must be named `claude_desktop_config.json` even in VS Code
options.why: VS Code reads `.vscode/mcp.json` (or its user-level config).

options.text: VS Code requires every server to be published in the MCP Registry
options.why: Local servers need no registry entry.

explanation: Hosts share concepts but not file formats. VS Code's `mcp.json` has a `servers` object mapping names to configurations (with `type`, `command`, `args`, `env`, or `url` for HTTP) and an optional `inputs` array for secrets. Claude Desktop and Claude Code use `mcpServers`.

stem: A team shares `.vscode/mcp.json` in git. One server needs each developer's personal API key. Which approach fits VS Code's configuration format?

options.text: Commit the key in the `env` block, since the repository is private
options.why: Never commit credentials, even to private repositories.

options.text: Put the key in the server's `args` so it is not stored in `env`
options.why: It is still committed, and command lines are visible in process listings.

options.text: Ask the model to request the key from the user in chat at runtime
options.why: Secrets must stay out of the model's context.

options.text: Use an `inputs` entry and reference `${input:api-key}` in `env`
options.why: Correct: VS Code prompts for the value on first start and stores it securely.

explanation: VS Code's `inputs` array defines input variables, for example `{"type": "promptString", "id": "api-key", "description": "API key", "password": true}`. Referencing `${input:api-key}` makes VS Code prompt the first time the server starts and store the value securely, so the shared file holds no secret.

stem: The MCP Inspector's web launcher prints a URL that contains a token, and the docs say to open that URL instead of typing `localhost:6274` from memory. Why does the token exist?

options.text: It is a licence key that unlocks the Inspector's full feature set
options.why: The Inspector is open source and has no licence keys.

options.text: It is the OAuth access token that the Inspector sends to your MCP server
options.why: OAuth tokens come from the server's authorization server and live in the secret store.

options.text: It guards a backend that can spawn processes on your machine
options.why: Correct: the per-launch token stands between that capability and anything else that can reach the port.

options.text: It identifies your browser tab so several people can share one Inspector session
options.why: It is a security gate, not a collaboration feature.

explanation: The web client is backed by a Node server that owns MCP connections and can start stdio processes. Every `/api/*` route requires the per-launch bearer token. The backend binds `127.0.0.1` by default, and `DANGEROUSLY_OMIT_AUTH=true` disables the check, which is only safe where nothing else can reach the port.

stem: Match each MCP Inspector web tab with what you would use it for.

options.text: Console
options.why: The stdio server process's stderr.

options.text: Network
options.why: The raw HTTP view: status, headers and bodies.

options.text: Protocol
options.why: The JSON-RPC transcript of requests, responses and notifications.

options.text: Tools
options.why: Browse schemas, fill in arguments and call a tool.

prompts.text: A stdio server dies at startup and you want its stack trace
A Streamable HTTP server returns 400 and you want to see the headers
You want to see the exact `tools/call` request and its result as JSON-RPC
You want to try a tool by hand with specific arguments

explanation: Console appears for stdio servers and Network for HTTP or SSE servers (never both). Protocol is always present and shows JSON-RPC traffic; Tools appears when the server has the `tools` capability. For a stdio server that fails for no visible reason, the recipes say to check the Console first.

stem:
Complete the MCP Inspector CLI command that prints a local server's tools and exits:

```bash
npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector --cli node build/index.js --method ____
```

Type the method name.
explanation: The CLI connects, runs the one request named by `--method`, prints the result and exits, which suits CI and coding agents. Other methods include `tools/call` (with `--tool-name` and `--tool-arg`), `resources/read` (with `--uri`) and `prompts/get`. `--format json` emits clean JSON for piping into `jq`.

stem: Your custom client calls a tool through the Python SDK, and the tool's code raises an exception on the server. What does the client code see, and what should it do?

options.text: A Python exception from `call_tool`, which the client should catch and hide from the model
options.why: A failing tool does not raise on the client, and hiding the failure prevents recovery.

options.text: A `CallToolResult` with the error flag set; pass the error text and flag to the model
options.why: Correct: tool failures come back as results with `is_error` so the model can adjust.

options.text: A dropped connection, after which the client must restart the server process
options.why: A tool error is an ordinary result; the connection stays up.

options.text: An empty result, because the SDK silently discards failed calls
options.why: The error content is returned, not discarded.

explanation: Tool execution errors are reported inside the result (`isError: true`, `is_error` in the Python client), not as transport failures. The official client tutorial forwards that flag to the model as the tool result's error state so the model can read the message and try something else.

stem:
This entry in a project's `.mcp.json` is ignored by Claude Code, which reports a configuration error. Why?

```json
{"mcpServers": {"docs": {"url": "https://docs.example.com/mcp"}}}
```

options.text: Remote servers can only be added with `claude mcp add`, never in `.mcp.json`
options.why: `.mcp.json` supports remote servers with `type` and `url`.

options.text: The URL must end in `/sse` for Claude Code to accept it
options.why: Streamable HTTP endpoints need no particular path.

options.text: With no `type`, Claude Code reads the entry as a stdio server, which has no command
options.why: Correct: add `"type": "http"` (or `sse` or `ws`) to the entry.

options.text: Project-scoped servers may not point at domains outside the repository's organisation
options.why: No such restriction exists.

explanation: Claude Code treats an entry without `type` as stdio. An entry with a `url` but no `type` is reported as a configuration error and skipped, with a message asking you to add `"type": "http"`. The `type` field also accepts `streamable-http` as an alias for `http`.

stem: A teammate clones a repository whose `.mcp.json` defines two servers. In their interactive Claude Code session the servers do not connect yet, and `claude mcp list` shows them as pending approval. What is going on?

options.text: Claude Code asks before using project-scoped servers from `.mcp.json`, for security
options.why: Correct: the user reviews and approves them in an interactive session.

options.text: `.mcp.json` only takes effect after an administrator signs the file
options.why: There is no signing step.

options.text: Project-scoped servers load only after a restart of the operating system
options.why: No restart is involved.

options.text: The servers are missing from the teammate's `~/.claude.json`, which must mirror `.mcp.json`
options.why: Project scope exists precisely so teammates do not have to copy entries.

explanation: Because a repository could ship a malicious server, Claude Code prompts for approval in interactive sessions before using project-scoped servers, and a cloned repository cannot approve its own servers through committed settings in an untrusted folder. `claude mcp reset-project-choices` resets earlier choices.

stem: A shared `.mcp.json` contains `"headers": {"Authorization": "Bearer ${DOCS_TOKEN}"}`. A developer who never set `DOCS_TOKEN` starts Claude Code. What happens?

options.text: Claude Code refuses to load the whole `.mcp.json` file
options.why: The config still loads.

options.text: Claude Code prompts for the value and stores it in the keychain
options.why: That describes VS Code `inputs`, not `${VAR}` expansion.

options.text: Claude Code silently drops the header and connects without it
options.why: The header is sent, just unexpanded.

options.text: It warns and sends the literal `${DOCS_TOKEN}` text
options.why: Correct: unset variables without a default stay unexpanded, with a missing-variable warning.

explanation: `.mcp.json` supports `${VAR}` and `${VAR:-default}` in `command`, `args`, `env`, `url` and `headers`. If a variable is unset and has no default, the config still loads, `claude mcp list` shows a warning for that server, and the `${VAR}` text is used as-is. Set the variable or give a default.

stem: The same server name is defined in several places. Order the sources from highest to lowest precedence in Claude Code (ignoring organisation-managed servers).

options.text: Plugin-provided servers
Project scope (`.mcp.json`)
claude.ai connectors
Local scope (`~/.claude.json`, current project)
User scope (`~/.claude.json`, all projects)

explanation: Claude Code connects once, using the whole entry from the highest-precedence source; fields are not merged across scopes. Scopes are matched by name, while plugins and connectors are matched by endpoint. Servers an organisation provides through managed settings rank above all of these.

stem: A server runs fine from your terminal, but Claude Desktop shows it as failed. Which of these are plausible causes, according to the official troubleshooting guidance? (Choose three.)

options.text: A relative path in `command` or `args`
options.why: The working directory under the host may be undefined, so use absolute paths.

options.text: Invalid JSON in `claude_desktop_config.json`, such as a trailing comma
options.why: Configuration syntax errors are a listed startup problem.

options.text: An environment variable the server needs is not set in the entry's `env`
options.why: Stdio servers inherit only a limited environment.

options.text: The server writes its logs to stderr
options.why: That is correct behaviour; stdout is the one to keep clean.

options.text: The server uses stdio instead of Streamable HTTP
options.why: Claude Desktop config launches stdio servers; that is the expected transport.

options.text: The config file lists more than one server
options.why: Multiple entries under `mcpServers` are normal.

explanation: The debugging guide groups startup failures into path issues (wrong executable path, relative paths), configuration errors (invalid JSON, missing fields) and environment problems (missing variables). The fastest checks are the logs, running the exact command by hand, and testing the server in the Inspector.

stem: You built a server that speaks only revision 2026-07-28. In the MCP Inspector the connection fails, and the Protocol tab shows an `initialize` request. What should you change?

options.text: Downgrade your server to the 2025-11-25 SDK, since the Inspector cannot speak 2026-07-28
options.why: The Inspector supports the modern era; it just does not use it by default.

options.text: Set the server's Protocol Era to `modern` or `auto`
options.why: Correct: `legacy` is the default, and it sends plain `initialize` without probing.

options.text: Add an `Mcp-Session-Id` header so the Inspector can resume the session
options.why: Sessions do not exist in 2026-07-28.

options.text: Switch the transport from Streamable HTTP to SSE
options.why: The era, not the transport, is the problem.

explanation: The Inspector treats protocol era as a per-server setting: `legacy` (the default, plain `initialize`), `auto` (probe `server/discover`, fall back to `initialize`) and `modern` (pin 2026-07-28 with no fallback). Legacy is the default because a debugging tool should not auto-probe.

stem: Order the steps a host or agent framework goes through to let a model use tools from an MCP server.

options.text: Send the user's message plus the tool definitions to the model
Add the tool result to the conversation and call the model again
Call `tools/list` and convert each tool into the model API's tool definition format
When the model returns a tool-use block, send `tools/call` to the server that owns the tool
Connect to the server and discover its capabilities

explanation: Frameworks such as LangChain's MCP adapters wrap exactly this loop: connect, list tools, convert MCP tool schemas into the framework's native tool type, and dispatch the model's tool calls back through the MCP client. The loop repeats until the model answers without requesting more tools.

stem: Your host's query function sends the conversation and tools to the model, executes every `tool_use` block in the response, sends the results back once, and prints the model's next text. Users report that multi-step tasks stop halfway. What is the bug?

options.text: It should call `tools/list` before every single tool call
options.why: Re-listing tools does not explain tasks stopping after one round.

options.text: The model must receive tool results as assistant messages, not user messages
options.why: Tool results go back in a user message; that part is right.

options.text: It never loops on `tool_use` blocks in later responses
options.why: Correct: the model may need several rounds of tool calls, so the host must keep looping.

options.text: It should send all tool calls to the server in one batched JSON-RPC array
options.why: Batching changes nothing about the missing loop.

explanation: The official quickstart client handles one round of tool calls for brevity. A production agent loop keeps calling the model and executing requested tools until the model stops asking for tools (or a step limit is reached), checking the error flag on each result along the way.

stem: According to the tools specification, which behaviours SHOULD a client or host implement? (Choose three.)

options.text: Prompt the user for confirmation on sensitive operations
options.why: Listed as a client SHOULD.

options.text: Show tool inputs to the user before calling the server, to avoid data exfiltration
options.why: Listed as a client SHOULD.

options.text: Validate tool results before passing them to the LLM
options.why: Listed as a client SHOULD.

options.text: Skip confirmation for any tool whose `readOnlyHint` is true, whatever server it comes from
options.why: Annotations are untrusted hints unless the server is trusted.

options.text: Approve all tools automatically once a server is added to the configuration
options.why: Adding a server is not consent to every call it might make.

options.text: Pass tool errors to the model only after removing every detail of what went wrong
options.why: Error details are what let the model recover.

explanation: The spec splits duties: servers MUST validate inputs, enforce access control, rate-limit invocations and sanitise outputs, while clients SHOULD confirm sensitive operations, show inputs before calling, validate results before the LLM sees them and follow the `$ref` resolution rules when validating.

stem: Match each responsibility with the component that owns it in an MCP deployment.

options.text: Host
options.why: The AI application: consent UI, model, and isolation between servers.

options.text: MCP client
options.why: One dedicated connection to one server.

options.text: MCP server
options.why: Exposes capabilities; validates its own inputs and enforces access control.

options.text: Authorization server
options.why: Authenticates users and issues access tokens for remote servers.

prompts.text: Asking the user to approve a destructive tool call before it runs
Maintaining the protocol connection to the GitHub server
Rejecting a `tools/call` whose arguments fail validation
Issuing the access token after the user signs in

explanation: The host coordinates everything the user sees, including approvals and keeping servers isolated from each other. It creates one client per server, and each client holds a dedicated connection. Servers must validate inputs and enforce their own access control. For remote servers, an OAuth authorization server issues the tokens the client presents.

stem: Claude Code exposes MCP tools to the model as `mcp__<server>__<tool>`. After you rename a server to a long descriptive name, one tool appears in `/mcp` but the model can never call it. What is the likely cause?

options.text: Its full prefixed name now exceeds 128 characters
options.why: Correct: shorten the server or tool name.

options.text: Renaming a server invalidates its OAuth tokens, which hides its tools
options.why: An auth problem would affect every tool from that server, and `/mcp` would flag it.

options.text: Tool names may not contain the server name, so the rename broke validation
options.why: The host adds the prefix itself; servers do not control it.

options.text: The server must send `notifications/tools/list_changed` after every rename
options.why: The rename happens in the client's configuration; the server's tool list did not change.

explanation: Hosts that aggregate servers disambiguate names by prefixing a server identifier, as the spec recommends (rather than relying on `serverInfo.name`, which is not unique). Prefixes lengthen names: the spec says tool names SHOULD be at most 128 characters, and Claude Code drops a tool whose full name exceeds 128 characters because the model API would reject the request.

stem: In programmatic tool calling (code mode), once the user approves a model-written script, every tool call the script makes at runtime is pre-approved.

options.text: True
options.why: Approving the script is not blanket approval; the broker still evaluates each call.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: the host broker must apply the same confirmation policy to sandbox-originated calls as to direct ones, though it may grant categorical approval such as one tool for one run.

explanation: In code mode the host is still the MCP host for spec purposes. Approving the script does not grant blanket approval for every tool call it makes. Hosts may grant categorical approval (for example, allow `ticketing_createIssue` for this script run), but the broker must evaluate each call against that grant.

stem: A teammate renames a required parameter in a tool's `inputSchema`. Which checks would catch this breaking change before release? (Choose two.)

options.text: A contract test that snapshots the `tools/list` output and fails when a schema changes
options.why: Comparing the advertised schema against a known-good snapshot flags the rename.

options.text: A CI step that runs the Inspector CLI with `--method tools/list --format json` and asserts the expected parameter with `jq`
options.why: This exercises the real protocol surface the hosts will see.

options.text: Unit tests that call the Python handler function directly with keyword arguments
options.why: They test the function, which the teammate updated too; they never look at the advertised schema.

options.text: Asking a colleague to try the server once in Claude Desktop
options.why: Manual and unrepeatable; easy to miss a renamed field.

options.text: Checking that the server process starts without errors
options.why: The server starts fine; the contract is what changed.

explanation: Test layers catch different failures: unit tests cover handler logic, in-memory client tests and contract or snapshot tests cover the protocol surface (names, schemas, error shapes), and evaluations cover whether models pick and use tools correctly. The Inspector CLI's JSON output and exit codes are designed for CI gates like this.

stem: A CI job runs `mcp-inspector --cli "$URL" --transport http --method tools/list` against an OAuth-protected server. It must never hang or open a browser, should reuse a token obtained earlier, and should fail clearly otherwise. Which change meets all three?

options.text: Set `DANGEROUSLY_OMIT_AUTH=true` so the CLI skips authorization
options.why: That variable disables the web backend's own token check; it does not authenticate you to the MCP server.

options.text: Add `--stored-auth-only` and check for exit code 3
options.why: Correct: it uses a stored token if present and fails fast otherwise, without interactive OAuth.

options.text: Pipe `yes` into the command so every OAuth prompt is accepted
options.why: The browser-based flow still needs a human to sign in.

options.text: Add `--format json`, which makes the CLI non-interactive
options.why: Output format does not change authorization behaviour.

explanation: By default the CLI runs the loopback OAuth flow. `--stored-auth-only` never starts interactive OAuth or step-up and never opens a browser; it uses the shared token store or fails with `auth_required`. Exit codes separate failure classes: 3 for authentication, 4 for unreachable, 5 for a tool error, and a JSON error envelope goes to stderr.

stem: Your host uses progressive tool discovery and adds newly found tool definitions to the `tools` array mid-conversation. Token costs rise instead of falling. What is the likely cause, and what is the recommended fix?

options.text: Discovery itself is costly; load every tool up front instead
options.why: Loading hundreds of definitions up front is the problem progressive discovery solves.

options.text: Changing `tools` breaks prompt caching; append after the cache breakpoint
options.why: Correct: keeping the prefix stable preserves the cache.

options.text: The server's `ttlMs` is too short, so the host re-lists tools every turn
options.why: Server-side caching hints do not explain cache misses at the model provider.

options.text: Tool descriptions are too long; truncate them to one word each
options.why: Truncation hurts selection and does not fix cache invalidation.

explanation: Most providers cache the prompt prefix, including the `tools` array. Adding or removing definitions mid-conversation invalidates that cache, and the miss can cost more than the definitions saved. The client best practices suggest appending new definitions after the cache breakpoint rather than re-sorting, or using a stable meta-tool, and treating server disconnection as a conversation-boundary operation.

stem: Your host connects to ten MCP servers. One of them starts timing out on every call. Which architecture keeps the other nine working and the model informed?

options.text: One client per server; mark the slow one's tools unavailable to the model
options.why: Correct: the failure stays contained to one client.

options.text: A single shared MCP client that multiplexes all ten servers over one connection, so one reconnect fixes everything
options.why: MCP clients hold one connection to one server, and sharing would spread the failure.

options.text: Retry the slow server's calls in a loop until it answers, holding the model's turn open
options.why: This blocks the conversation and still gives the model no information.

options.text: Restart all ten server processes whenever any one of them times out
options.why: This punishes the healthy servers and loses their in-flight work.

explanation: A host creates one MCP client per server, and each client keeps a dedicated connection. That isolation means one server's failure, re-authorization or restart does not affect the others. A good host surfaces the failure to the model (for example, by reporting the tools as unavailable) instead of hanging or silently dropping calls.

stem: You add programmatic tool calling (code mode) to your host. Which safeguards do the client best practices call for? (Choose three.)

options.text: The sandbox has no direct network access; all calls go through the host broker
options.why: The broker is where authorization and access control are enforced.

options.text: API keys and tokens stay in the host; generated code only calls typed functions
options.why: Credentials must never be exposed to model-written code.

options.text: Sandbox output is validated and truncated before it goes back to the model
options.why: Output filtering is listed among the security considerations.

options.text: Server tokens are passed into the sandbox as environment variables so the code can call servers directly
options.why: That exposes credentials and bypasses the broker.

options.text: Results from server A are treated as trusted input to server B, because both are behind the same host
options.why: Cross-server results are untrusted input and get the same review as direct calls.

options.text: Timeouts are skipped so long scripts can finish
options.why: Resource limits (timeouts, memory) are required to stop runaway scripts.

explanation: In code mode the host turns tool schemas into typed functions inside a sandbox and brokers every call to the MCP servers. The guidance: no sandbox network access, no credential exposure, per-call authorization, cross-server data treated as untrusted, resource limits, and output filtering before anything reaches the model.

stem: In your code-mode host, a generated wrapper calls `tools/call` and the server returns a successful JSON-RPC response with `isError: true`. The model-written script continues as if the call worked and files a bogus ticket. What should the wrapper do?

options.text: Retry the call until `isError` becomes false
options.why: Blind retries can repeat side effects and may never succeed.

options.text: Turn `isError: true` into a thrown exception
options.why: Correct: model-written code can then use try/catch, and the model can self-correct.

options.text: Treat it as a transport failure and restart the MCP server
options.why: It is a tool-level error, not a transport failure.

options.text: Drop the result and return `null`, so the script does not crash
options.why: Silent nulls are how the bogus ticket got filed.

explanation: MCP tool errors arrive as successful responses with `isError: true`, not as transport failures. The best practices say generated wrappers should turn this into a thrown exception, and if an uncaught error ends the script, surface it as the result so the model can self-correct and report partial side effects.

stem: A colleague wants to reach your MCP Inspector web UI from another machine. Which setups keep it safe? (Choose two.)

options.text: Keep the default `127.0.0.1` bind and connect through an SSH tunnel
options.why: The backend stays on loopback, and only people with SSH access reach it.

options.text: Put an authenticating reverse proxy in front of it on a private network
options.why: A real access-control boundary in front of the backend is the documented approach.

options.text: Bind `0.0.0.0` and set `DANGEROUSLY_OMIT_AUTH=true` so the colleague needs no token
options.why: Anyone who can reach the port could then spawn processes as you.

options.text: Run the Docker image with a bare `-p 6274:6274`
options.why: A bare publish exposes the backend, and the page that discloses its token, on every host interface.

options.text: Rely on the origin allow-list to keep non-browser clients out
options.why: Requests with no `Origin` header, such as curl, skip that check.

explanation: The web backend can spawn processes, and `GET /` discloses its token, so the bind address matters more than the token. The docs say never to combine `DANGEROUSLY_OMIT_AUTH` with a non-loopback bind; use an authenticating reverse proxy, an SSH tunnel or a private network, and publish Docker ports as `127.0.0.1:6274:6274`.

stem: You run the MCP Inspector on a headless Linux CI box with no keychain. Which statements about where it keeps secrets are correct? (Choose two.)

options.text: It falls back automatically to `~/.mcp-inspector/secrets.json`, unencrypted unless you supply a key
options.why: The fallback is automatic, and the only signs are a stderr warning and a footer in the web client's settings dialogs.

options.text: Setting `MCP_INSPECTOR_SECRET_STORE=memory` keeps secrets out of files, at the cost of re-entering them each session
options.why: The memory store is one of the documented ways to avoid the plaintext file.

options.text: Header values in `mcp.json`, such as a static `Authorization` header, are moved to the secret store
options.why: Headers are not secrets; they are saved in `mcp.json` as written.

options.text: Encrypting the file protects secrets even from stdio servers that the Inspector starts as the same user
options.why: Code running as the same user can read the key or process memory; encryption only helps if the file leaks on its own.

options.text: The file is safe to commit, because its mode is `0600`
options.why: File mode protects against other local users, not against anyone holding a copy.

explanation: Secrets (OAuth tokens, client secrets, stdio `env:` values) go to the OS keychain when one exists, otherwise to a `secrets.json` file that is plaintext unless keyed. Remedies: restore a keychain, encrypt with `MCP_INSPECTOR_SECRET_KEY_FILE`, or use the memory store. Stdio servers run as you and are not isolated from these files.

stem:
Your server takes its own `--config` flag. This Inspector CLI run treats `--config` as the Inspector's flag and fails:

```bash
mcp-inspector --cli node build/index.js --config /etc/srv.conf --method tools/list
```

Which command passes the flag to the server?

options.text: `mcp-inspector --cli node build/index.js -- --config /etc/srv.conf --method tools/list`
options.why: In the CLI, everything after `--` belongs to the Inspector, so `--config` would still be read as its flag.

options.text: `mcp-inspector node build/index.js -- --config /etc/srv.conf --cli --method tools/list`
options.why: Mode flags count only at the front, so this launches the web client and hands everything after `--`, including `--cli`, to the server.

options.text: `mcp-inspector --cli node build/index.js --config /etc/srv.conf -- --method tools/list`
options.why: Correct: in the CLI, everything before `--` is the target and everything after is the Inspector's own options.

options.text: `mcp-inspector --cli --config /etc/srv.conf node build/index.js --method tools/list`
options.why: Here `--config` is the Inspector's read-only config-file flag, which cannot be combined with an ad-hoc target.

explanation: The Inspector's web and TUI clients pass everything after a bare `--` to the server. The CLI splits the other way: everything before `--` is the target and everything after is the Inspector's options, so a server that takes flags needs the separator after its arguments.

stem: In Claude Code you configured a remote server with `"headers": {"Authorization": "Bearer ..."}`. The token has expired, and the server answers 401. What does Claude Code do?

options.text: It discards the header and starts the server's OAuth flow automatically
options.why: Claude Code does not fall back to OAuth when your configured header is rejected.

options.text: It reports a failed connection; no OAuth fallback
options.why: Correct: the credential to fix is the one you configured.

options.text: It retries every few seconds until the server accepts the header
options.why: Retrying an expired token cannot succeed.

options.text: It asks the model to request a new token from the user in chat
options.why: Credentials never go through the model.

explanation: Claude Code flags a remote server for sign-in on 401 or 403 when it can fix the problem through OAuth. For a server whose `Authorization` header you configured (in `headers` or through a `headersHelper`), a 401 or 403 is reported as a failed connection instead, because the configured credential is what needs fixing.

stem: A project's `.mcp.json` sends `"Authorization": "Bearer ${ANTHROPIC_API_KEY}"` to a remote MCP server. The variable is set in your shell, yet the server gets `Bearer ` with no token and returns 401. Why?

options.text: Claude Code only expands variables in `command` and `args`, never in `headers`
options.why: Expansion works in `headers` and `url` for names outside the protected set.

options.text: Variables in `.mcp.json` must be written as `$ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` without braces
options.why: The supported syntax is `${VAR}` and `${VAR:-default}`.

options.text: Claude Code blanks its own credentials in remote headers
options.why: Correct: copy the value into a variable with your own name if the server really needs it.

options.text: The shell variable is only read when Claude Code is started with `--debug`
options.why: Debug mode does not affect expansion.

explanation: To stop a repository's `.mcp.json` or a plugin from exfiltrating credentials, Claude Code reads names such as `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, `ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN` and cloud-provider tokens as empty in a remote server's `url` and `headers`, whether or not they are set, and ignores `:-default` on them. Other names, such as `API_KEY`, expand as written.

stem: Your server has a `grant_access` tool whose whole point is that a person approves every call, even when a user runs Claude Code in a permissive mode such as `bypassPermissions`. Which server-side option guarantees a permission prompt in Claude Code?

options.text: Set `annotations.destructiveHint: true`, which forces confirmation in every client
options.why: Annotations are hints; permissive modes and allow rules can still auto-approve.

options.text: Ask for confirmation through form-mode elicitation inside the tool
options.why: Claude Code's `Elicitation` hook can answer elicitations automatically, so no human is guaranteed.

options.text: Return `isError: true` on the first call so the user must retry by hand
options.why: An error is not a consent step, and the model can simply retry.

options.text: Set `_meta["anthropic/requiresUserInteraction"]: true`
options.why: Correct: Claude Code then prompts on every call, even in permissive modes, and allow rules cannot skip it.

explanation: Claude Code honours `_meta["anthropic/requiresUserInteraction"]: true` (a JSON boolean) on a tool: it shows the permission prompt on every call, including in `acceptEdits`, `auto` and `bypassPermissions` modes, offers no "don't ask again" option, and denies the call in `dontAsk` mode. Standard annotations remain untrusted hints that hosts may treat as they like.

stem: With Claude Code's MCP tool search enabled, the model rarely discovers your server's tools for relevant tasks, even though the tool descriptions are good. What change helps most?

options.text: Raise `MAX_MCP_OUTPUT_TOKENS`, so that more of your server's tool definitions fit
options.why: That limits tool output size, not discovery.

options.text: Split each tool into several narrower tools, so more names show up in search
options.why: More overlapping tools usually makes selection worse.

options.text: Write clear server instructions about what your tools do
options.why: Correct: they help the model decide when to search for your tools.

options.text: Rename every tool to start with `search_`, so the search tool ranks them first
options.why: Misleading names hurt selection and do not describe when to use the tools.

explanation: With tool search, only tool names and server instructions load at session start; full definitions are fetched on demand. Server instructions therefore work like a skill description: they tell the model what category of tasks your tools cover. The broader levers for tool selection are clear names and descriptions and fewer overlapping tools.
